Name: linguistic_cost_of_thought
Title: The Linguistic Cost of Thought: Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering for Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM reasons through harder sub-steps, it dynamically suppresses surface-language identity in favor of a language-agnostic representation; the momentary degree of this suppression is a readable, causal signal of reasoning difficulty and correctness, and selectively increasing suppression only at high-difficulty steps improves reasoning more than blanket language-component ablation.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs develop a compact language-agnostic core (Emergence of Abstract Thought, 2025), route reasoning through English-shaped space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025), and that static, blanket ablation of language-specific activations improves multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). Others study language mixing as a latent-preference symptom (Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs, 2025) and knowledge-free reasoning transfer (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners, 2024). All existing interventions are static/global: they remove or preserve language components uniformly across a generation. Our proposal is distinct in three ways: (1) we treat language-agnosticism as a time-varying per-step signal (a 'linguistic cost' meter) rather than a fixed property; (2) we causally test whether difficulty predicts this signal via truncation and error-injection at the step level; and (3) we introduce a difficulty-gated steering intervention that increases language-agnosticism only at hard steps, contrasting it head-to-head with blanket ablation. No prior work links the dynamics of language suppression to step-level difficulty or uses it as an adaptive controller.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work reveals that large language models (LLMs) maintain a compact language-agnostic representational core underlying cross-lingual generalization, and that suppressing surface-language components can improve multilingual reasoning. However, these interventions are static, applying uniform treatment across an entire generation. We hypothesize that language-agnosticism is instead dynamic: an LLM temporarily 'sheds' its surface language when a reasoning sub-step becomes hard, and this momentary shedding is a readable and causal signal of reasoning difficulty and correctness. We define a per-step Language-Agnosticism Score (LAS) from the projection of hidden states onto a language-identity subspace estimated from parallel data. First, we characterize the dynamics of LAS across chain-of-thought steps and test whether it rises with step-level difficulty using truncation and controlled error-injection probes. Second, we test whether LAS at intermediate steps predicts final-answer correctness, yielding a lightweight self-monitoring signal. Third, we introduce Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering (DG-LAS), which increases language-agnosticism only at steps flagged as high-difficulty, and compare it against blanket ablation and no-intervention baselines on multilingual math and commonsense reasoning across typologically diverse languages and several open-weight models. We expect DG-LAS to match or exceed blanket ablation while preserving fluency and reducing the fluency degradation that global ablation causes on easy steps. Our work reframes language suppression from a static property to a dynamic, controllable resource, offering both an interpretable difficulty meter and a training-free intervention.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Language-identity subspace construction and validation): This prerequisite builds the meter the rest of the study reads. Data: FLORES-200 (an existing professionally-translated parallel corpus; 997 sentences in its dev split are available in every language), used as is; we take all ~997 dev sentences in 8 typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Russian, Chinese, Japanese, Swahili), ~7,976 sentence instances. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Aya-23-8B, all pretrained weights frozen; we fit only an external linear classifier. For each layer we extract the final-token residual-stream vector and fit an 8-way L2-regularized logistic-regression language classifier (5-fold cross-validation, seeds 0/1/2); its top three directions define the language-identity subspace, and LAS(token,layer)=1 minus the L2-normalized projection magnitude of the hidden state onto that subspace (higher = more language-agnostic). Systems compared: per-layer classifier vs. a shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: held-out language-classification accuracy (chance = 12.5%); then transfer accuracy on 500 held-out Tatoeba parallel sentences. Convincing result: at least one middle layer reaches >=85% held-out accuracy and >=80% Tatoeba transfer while the shuffled control stays at chance, establishing a content-orthogonal identity subspace. Indecision band: 40-85% held-out accuracy - the subspace only weakly separates languages, LAS becomes a noisy meter, and we would restrict every downstream analysis to the single best layer and report reduced power. Negative result (<40%, or no layer beating the shuffled control): no readable language-identity subspace exists, LAS is undefined, and the dynamic-shedding hypothesis cannot be tested as framed.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Reasoning difficulty raises momentary language-shedding): Tests the claim that LAS rises with step-level difficulty. Data: MGSM (existing; 250 GSM-style problems per language, human-translated) across the 8 languages above = 2,000 problems, and XCOPA (existing; 500 validation items per language) for the commonsense arm across its overlapping languages; used as is. We segment each generated chain-of-thought into steps by newline/sentence and arithmetic-operation boundaries. Models: same three, frozen; greedy decoding plus 5 samples/problem (temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2) for stability. Systems compared: per-step LAS regressed on two difficulty proxies - token surprisal under the same model, and operation complexity (operand count/carries for math). Decisive metric first: the standardized regression coefficient of step difficulty on step LAS in a mixed-effects model (LAS ~ difficulty + step_position + (1|problem) + (1|model)); secondary: Spearman correlation per model. Convincing result: a positive difficulty coefficient with 95% bootstrap CI excluding zero in at least 2 of 3 models, robust to controlling for step position and length. Indecision band: standardized coefficient in [-0.05, 0.05] with CI spanning zero - difficulty does not measurably move LAS, so the 'linguistic cost' meter is not difficulty-sensitive and H1 is unsupported at this resolution. Negative result (significant negative coefficient): the model becomes MORE language-anchored on hard steps, contradicting the shedding hypothesis. Evidence is planned, not measured.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Causal difficulty manipulation): Isolates difficulty from confounds by intervening on it. Data: a built set of 300 MGSM-derived items (drawn from the 2,000 above) each rendered in two forms - (a) truncated CoT fed back so the model must complete a genuinely hard remaining step, and (b) a single interior step corrupted by a controlled arithmetic error requiring recovery - plus matched easy-step controls; ~1,200 constructed trials. Models: same three, frozen. Systems compared: LAS at the manipulated hard/error-recovery step vs. matched easy step, within item. Decisive metric first: within-item LAS difference (hard minus easy), tested with a paired bootstrap. Convincing result: mean LAS spike at genuinely hard/error-recovery steps with 95% CI excluding zero and effect size (Cohen's d) >=0.3 in at least 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: |d|<0.15 with CI crossing zero - the causal manipulation does not reliably move LAS, meaning any correlation in Experiment 2 is likely driven by uncontrolled length/position rather than difficulty per se. Negative result (LAS drops at manipulated hard steps): shedding is not caused by difficulty.

Experiment 4 (H2 - LAS predicts final correctness): Tests that intermediate-step LAS is a readable self-monitoring signal. Data: the 2,000 MGSM problems, each with 8 sampled trajectories labeled correct/incorrect by exact match = ~16,000 labeled trajectories; we hold out 30% of problems for testing (no problem overlap). Models: same three, frozen; the only trainable component is a lightweight logistic probe on aggregated intermediate-step LAS features (mean/max/slope), seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: LAS probe vs. baselines - answer-token confidence, predictive entropy, and logit-lens English-routing degree. Decisive metric first: AUROC for predicting final correctness on held-out problems. Convincing result: LAS-probe AUROC >=0.65 and statistically above the confidence/entropy baselines (DeLong test, 95% CI on the AUROC gap excluding zero) in at least 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] or overlapping the baselines' CIs - LAS carries weak, non-additive correctness information and is not a useful monitor on its own. Negative result (AUROC <=0.55): LAS does not predict correctness, refuting the self-monitoring claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering beats blanket ablation): Tests the central intervention claim. Data: a held-out MGSM split of 800 problems across the 8 languages (kept separate from probe training). Models: same three, frozen; steering adds -alpha times the language-identity component to the residual stream in middle layers only at flagged steps; alpha and gate threshold tuned on a 200-item dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared, four conditions: (i) no intervention, (ii) blanket ablation (prior state of the art; language component removed at every step), (iii) random-gated steering matched for number of intervened steps (control isolating the gating contribution), and (iv) DG-LAS (steer only at steps flagged high-difficulty by surprisal threshold or the Experiment-4 probe). Decisive metric first: exact-match accuracy per language (macro-averaged); secondary: output fluency (perplexity under an external LM plus a GPT-judge rating on a 200-sample subset) and answer-in-target-language rate. Convincing result: DG-LAS matches or exceeds blanket ablation on accuracy (its 95% bootstrap CI lower bound at or above blanket ablation) AND shows higher fluency / lower easy-step degradation than blanket ablation, while beating random-gated steering by >=1 accuracy point. Indecision band: DG-LAS within +/-1.0 accuracy point of blanket ablation with overlapping fluency CIs - difficulty-gating yields no measurable advantage over blanket treatment, so the adaptive-controller motivation is not supported even if the meter is real. Negative result (DG-LAS below no-intervention or below random-gated): selective language-shedding does not help and may hurt.

Experiment 6 (Robustness - ablations): Data/models as above. We sweep layer choice, gating threshold, and steering strength alpha, and test cross-language generalization of the identity subspace (fit on 6 languages, evaluate LAS and DG-LAS on 2 held-out languages). Decisive metric: stability of the Experiment-2 difficulty coefficient and the Experiment-5 accuracy gap across settings. Convincing result: the sign and significance of both hold across a majority of layer/threshold settings and transfer to held-out languages. Indecision band: results flip sign across reasonable settings - findings are setting-specific and we report them as such. Negative result: effects vanish off the tuned operating point, indicating overfitting rather than a robust mechanism. All quantities above are planned evidence, not measured outcomes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The language-identity subspace may entangle content with language, confounding LAS; we mitigate with parallel-data controls and orthogonalization. Step segmentation is noisy for languages with weak CoT structure. Difficulty proxies (surprisal) may not reflect true reasoning difficulty. Difficulty-gated steering could destabilize generation or reduce fluency if applied too aggressively; strength/threshold tuning is required. Gains may be model- or language-specific and small on high-resource languages. Causal claims from steering are correlational unless carefully controlled, so we include random-gated and blanket baselines to isolate the difficulty-gating contribution.

Name: syntax_engine_reuse
Title: Is the Syntax Engine the Reasoning Engine? Testing Whether Hierarchical Language Circuits Power Non-Linguistic Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: The localizable components an LLM uses to process hierarchical linguistic structure are causally reused as a general-purpose 'structure engine' for non-linguistic hierarchical reasoning (arithmetic parsing, nested logic, code, formal grammars); ablating these syntax-specific components will degrade hierarchically-structured reasoning far more than flat/linear reasoning, revealing that syntactic machinery is a substrate for AI intelligence rather than a language-only module.
Related Work: Prior work (Disjoint Processing Mechanisms of Hierarchical and Linear Grammars, 2025) localized distinct hierarchy-selective components in LLMs and showed they fire on nonce words, but only ever tested them on *language* grammaticality judgments. Understanding Syntax in LLMs (2025) documents that LLMs fail on deep center-embedding. LLMs are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners (2023) and Do LLMs Understand Logic (2024) show reasoning relies on semantic/probabilistic associations, not symbolic rules, but do not connect this to syntactic circuitry. Syntactic-surprisal/garden-path psycholinguistics work (Hale 2001; van Schijndel & Linzen 2021) links parsing cost to processing difficulty in language only. No prior work asks whether the *identified hierarchical-syntax circuit* is causally recruited for non-linguistic reasoning that requires parsing nested structure (arithmetic order-of-operations, nested boolean logic, balanced parentheses, code AST depth). We uniquely bridge the syntax-localization literature and the reasoning literature by causally testing cross-domain reuse of a language circuit.
Abstract: Large language models process hierarchical linguistic structure using distinct, localizable components that fire even on meaningless (nonce) words, suggesting a syntax-specialized 'structure engine.' Separately, reasoning research shows LLMs solve nested arithmetic, logic, and code tasks that all require parsing hierarchical structure. We ask a simple question that connects language to intelligence: is the same hierarchical-syntax circuit reused when the model reasons over non-linguistic hierarchical structure? We first localize hierarchy-selective components using linguistic center-embedding contrasts (following established methods), identifying attention heads and MLP neurons whose ablation selectively degrades hierarchical over linear grammaticality judgments. We then test, without any additional fitting, whether ablating this *language-derived* circuit disproportionately harms performance on four non-linguistic tasks that vary in structural depth: order-of-operations arithmetic, nested boolean logic, balanced-parenthesis validation, and depth-varying code evaluation. Our central prediction is a depth-by-ablation interaction: ablating syntax components hurts deep/nested instances far more than flat instances, while control ablations (random components, or components selective for lexical/semantic features) do not. We further test the converse direction: fine-tuning on deep nested-structure reasoning should strengthen the *linguistic* hierarchy circuit measured on held-out sentences. Across several open-weight models we quantify circuit overlap (Jaccard of causally-important components), the accuracy-vs-depth ablation curves, and transfer of circuit strengthening. If confirmed, this reframes syntactic competence as a shared computational substrate for structured reasoning; if refuted, it shows the structure engine is domain-specific, both outcomes being informative for how language relates to machine intelligence.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Hierarchy-selective circuit localization): Prerequisite that identifies the language-derived circuit whose reuse the study tests. Data: minimal-pair grammaticality contrasts of center-embedding (hierarchical) vs. linear/positional grammars in English and Italian plus nonce/Jabberwocky variants, following the Disjoint-Processing minimal-pair design; we adapt that existing paradigm and construct 1,500 matched pairs (500 English, 500 Italian, 500 nonce), length-matched across the hierarchical/linear conditions. Models: Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3.1-8B, all weights frozen; localization uses activation patching and single-component (attention-head and MLP-neuron) mean-ablation, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: hierarchical vs. linear grammaticality accuracy under ablation of each component. Decisive metric first: the drop in hierarchical grammaticality accuracy minus the drop in linear accuracy for each ablated component (selectivity score). Convincing result: a rank-ordered set S_syn of components whose ablation drops hierarchical accuracy by >=10 points while sparing linear accuracy (selectivity CI excluding zero), reproducible across the two English/Italian sets. Indecision band: top-component selectivity in [0, 5] points - no component is convincingly hierarchy-specific, so S_syn is ill-defined and the reuse test loses its independent variable; we would then report that hierarchy processing is diffuse in these models. Negative result (no component beats random selectivity): the models lack a localizable syntax circuit, and the reuse hypothesis is untestable in them.

Experiment 2 (Setup - Control circuits): Data/models as above. We localize (a) linear/positional-selective components S_lin, (b) semantic/lexical-selective components S_sem via a synonym/antonym-and-category-membership contrast (500 built minimal pairs), and (c) random matched-size sets S_rand (10 draws). Decisive metric: each control set's own selectivity for its target contrast. Convincing result: S_lin and S_sem are each selective for their intended feature and largely disjoint from S_syn (Jaccard < 0.3). Indecision band: heavy overlap (Jaccard 0.3-0.6) between S_syn and controls - selectivity is muddy and later interaction tests must be read cautiously. Negative result: controls are indistinguishable from S_syn, undermining specificity claims.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Cross-domain reuse: depth-by-ablation interaction): Tests that ablating the syntax circuit disproportionately harms hierarchically-structured non-linguistic reasoning. Data: a constructed suite with controllable structural depth - order-of-operations arithmetic (nesting depth 0-5), nested boolean logic (depth 0-5), balanced-parenthesis validity (depth 1-8), and Python-expression evaluation (AST depth 1-6); ~2,000 items per task (8,000 total), balanced across depths and length-matched across depth bins to unconfound depth from sequence length. Models: same three, frozen; no additional fitting - S_syn/S_lin/S_sem/S_rand are transferred unchanged from Experiments 1-2. Systems compared: accuracy vs. depth under ablation of S_syn, S_lin, S_sem, S_rand, and no-ablation. Decisive metric first: the depth x ablation-set interaction coefficient from a mixed-effects logistic regression (accuracy ~ depth * ablation_set + (1|model) + (1|task)). Convincing result: the S_syn depth-slope is significantly steeper (more negative) than every control's, with 95% CI on the S_syn-minus-control interaction excluding zero in at least 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: S_syn interaction within the controls' CIs (difference CI spanning zero) - syntax-circuit ablation is no more depth-selective than random/semantic ablation, so cross-domain reuse is unsupported. Negative result (S_syn no steeper than no-ablation, or flat across depth): the syntax circuit is not recruited for non-linguistic hierarchy, i.e., the structure engine is domain-specific (an informative refutation of the headline claim).

Experiment 4 (H2 - Circuit-overlap above chance): Tests that non-linguistic reasoning independently recruits the same components. Data/models as Experiment 3. For each non-linguistic task we independently localize its causally-important components (activation patching on correct-vs-incorrect contrasts, 400 items/task). Systems compared: Jaccard overlap of each task's causal set with S_syn vs. with S_lin/S_sem/S_rand. Decisive metric first: Jaccard(task, S_syn) minus the mean Jaccard against the three controls. Convincing result: this excess overlap is positive with 95% bootstrap CI excluding zero for the deeper tasks, above the S_rand null distribution. Indecision band: excess overlap in [-0.05, 0.05] - reasoning does not preferentially reuse the syntax circuit though it may share diffuse machinery. Negative result (overlap at or below S_rand): no shared substrate.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Converse transfer): Tests that training on nested reasoning strengthens the linguistic hierarchy circuit. Data: 5,000 constructed deep nested-structure reasoning items (from the Experiment-3 generators, held out from evaluation) for LoRA fine-tuning; evaluation on 500 held-out center-embedding sentences never seen in training. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B; LoRA adapters trainable (rank 16, learning rate 1e-4, 3 epochs, seeds 0/1/2), base weights frozen. Systems compared: pre- vs. post-fine-tuning hierarchical grammaticality accuracy and S_syn ablation sensitivity, with a control LoRA fine-tuned on flat/linear reasoning matched for token count. Decisive metric first: change in S_syn ablation sensitivity (how much more S_syn ablation hurts hierarchical grammaticality after nested-reasoning training) relative to the flat-training control. Convincing result: nested-reasoning training increases S_syn sensitivity and held-out hierarchical accuracy significantly more than the flat-training control (95% CI on the difference excluding zero). Indecision band: difference CI spanning zero with |effect| < 2 points - transfer is too small to claim a shared, trainable circuit. Negative result (nested training does not strengthen, or weakens, the linguistic hierarchy circuit): the reuse is not bidirectional, weakening but not eliminating the substrate account. All effect sizes are reported with bootstrap CIs; every number here is planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Ablating syntax components may broadly degrade all outputs, masking the selective depth effect; we mitigate with matched-size random and semantic control ablations and by focusing on the *interaction* with depth rather than absolute drops. (2) Hierarchy-selective localization may be noisy or model-specific; we report multiple models and cross-validate localization on held-out sentence sets. (3) Non-linguistic tasks still pass through tokenization/language machinery, so 'non-linguistic' is relative; we use nonce-word controls and symbolic tokens to reduce semantic confounds. (4) Depth and difficulty may be confounded with sequence length; we length-match items across depths. (5) A null result (no cross-domain reuse) is still publishable as evidence that the structure engine is domain-specific, but weakens the headline claim. (6) LoRA transfer effects may be small; we power the experiment with sufficient items and report effect sizes with CIs.

Name: linguistic_cognitive_gear
Title: Language as a Cognitive Gear: Does Prompt Language Shift LLMs Between Intuitive and Reflective Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: The surface language of a prompt does not merely change an LLM's accuracy; it shifts the model along an intuition-vs-reflection axis, changing WHICH decision strategy it deploys on identical problems. Just as humans exhibit a 'Foreign Language Effect' where reasoning in a non-native language alters belief bias and cognitive-effort allocation, LLMs will show systematic, language-dependent shifts in susceptibility to intuitive lures (belief bias, base-rate neglect, CRT traps) that are not explained by accuracy or resource level alone, and this cognitive gear can be causally located and steered.
Related Work: Cognitive-science work documents a 'Foreign Language Effect': people show altered belief-bias and cognitive-effort allocation when reasoning in a foreign language (Thinking in a Foreign Language Distorts Allocation of Cognitive Effort, 2019). In LLMs, prior work shows (i) reasoning is routed through English latent space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025; Beyond English-Centric, 2024), (ii) language shapes causal-order biases (Under the Shadow of Babel / BICAUSE, 2025), (iii) accuracy gaps stem from understanding failures (Why Do Multilingual Reasoning Gaps Emerge?, 2025), and (iv) ablating language components boosts multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). All of these treat language as affecting ACCURACY, latent-routing, or a single bias type. None test whether surface language systematically changes the model's position on the general intuition-vs-reflection (System-1 vs System-2) axis across a battery of dual-process cognitive-bias tasks, whether such shifts are dissociable from accuracy and resource level, or whether the 'cognitive gear' is a locatable and steerable internal direction. We uniquely import the dual-process Foreign Language Effect framework into interpretability, providing a mechanism-level and causal account.
Abstract: Does an LLM reason with the same cognitive style regardless of the language it is prompted in? Cognitive science shows that humans reasoning in a foreign language allocate cognitive effort differently, altering their susceptibility to intuitive-but-wrong answers. We hypothesize an analogous phenomenon in LLMs: the surface language of a prompt acts as a 'cognitive gear,' shifting the model between fast intuitive answering and slow reflective reasoning on identical problems. Crucially, this is a claim about reasoning STRATEGY, not just accuracy. We assemble a multilingual battery of dual-process items where the intuitive answer diverges from the correct answer: belief-bias syllogisms, base-rate-neglect scenarios, Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) traps, and conjunction-fallacy items, each semantically matched and translated across typologically diverse languages. For each item we measure not just accuracy but the intuitive-response rate (rate of giving the tempting-but-wrong lure) and reflection engagement (spontaneous multi-step reasoning). We test whether the same model gives more intuitive-lure responses in some languages than others even when accuracy is controlled, and whether this dissociates from language resource level. We then probe mechanism: using a linear probe on hidden states we identify a 'reflection direction' separating intuitive-lure from reflective trajectories, test whether prompt language moves representations along it, and causally steer along it to override language-induced intuitive answering. Our study reframes multilingualism from an accuracy problem to a cognitive-style problem, offering the first dual-process, mechanistically-grounded account of how language shapes reasoning strategy in AI.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Multilingual dual-process battery): Prerequisite dataset. Data: a built battery of ~200 items per family across 4 families - belief-bias syllogisms (valid/invalid x believable/unbelievable), base-rate-neglect scenarios with a stereotype lure, expanded CRT-style traps, and conjunction-fallacy (Linda-style) items - 800 English source items, each with a labeled correct answer AND a labeled intuitive-lure answer, calibrated to mid-range difficulty. Translated into 8 typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Japanese) with back-translation quality checks and human spot-verification on a 10% sample, giving 6,400 language-item instances. Decisive metric first: back-translation match rate and human-judged adequacy. Convincing result: >=90% items pass adequacy in all languages; items failing are dropped and regenerated. Indecision band: 70-90% adequacy in some language - we retain only passing items and flag that language's reduced item count. Negative result (<70% in a language): that language is excluded to avoid confounding translation noise with strategy shifts.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Language shifts intuitive responding beyond accuracy): The central strategy-vs-accuracy test. Data: the 6,400 instances above, used as is. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B, all weights frozen; 5 samples/item at temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: the same model across the 8 languages. Decisive metric first: the Intuition Index = intuitive-lure response rate among errors (fraction of wrong answers matching the labeled lure vs. other wrong answers), analyzed in a mixed-effects model (lure_rate ~ language + per_language_accuracy + resource_level + (1|model) + (1|item)). Convincing result: language retains a significant effect on lure responding after controlling for per-language accuracy and a corpus-based resource-level covariate (likelihood-ratio test p and 95% CI on the language variance component excluding the accuracy-only model), replicated in at least 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: the language term explains <2% additional variance beyond accuracy with a CI touching zero - language differences are essentially accuracy-driven, so the cognitive-gear claim reduces to competence. Negative result (no language effect once accuracy is controlled): surface language does not move the intuition axis, refuting the hypothesis.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Reflection responsiveness by language): Tests the Foreign-Language-Effect analog that some languages carry more residual intuitive responding that reflection must correct. Data/models as Experiment 2. Systems compared: direct-answer vs. chain-of-thought prompting within each language. Decisive metric first: reflection responsiveness = reduction in lure rate from direct to CoT prompting, per language. Convincing result: languages differ significantly in residual (post-CoT) lure rate (mixed-effects language term CI excluding zero), mirroring cross-language effort differences. Indecision band: cross-language spread in residual lure rate < 3 points - reflection erases language differences, so any gear effect is superficial. Negative result: no language differences in reflection responsiveness.

Experiment 4 (H2 - A reflection direction exists and language moves representations along it): Tests the mechanistic locatability claim. Data: hidden states collected on items where the model answered intuitive-lure vs. reflective-correct (matched items, differing only in lure salience), from the 6,400 instances. Models: same four, frozen; trainable component is a per-layer linear probe (logistic, L2, seeds 0/1/2) separating lure from reflective trajectories; 70/30 item-disjoint train/test split. Systems compared: probe direction vs. random directions; and the projection of a fixed item's representation under different prompt languages. Decisive metric first: probe AUROC for lure-vs-reflective on held-out items; secondary: correlation between the per-item projection shift when switching prompt language and the per-item behavioral lure shift. Convincing result: probe AUROC >=0.70 at some layer AND a positive projection-shift-to-behavior correlation (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55,0.70] or projection-behavior correlation CI spanning zero - the 'reflection direction' is weak or not the axis language moves, so mechanism is unclear. Negative result (AUROC <=0.55): no linear reflection axis, undermining the mechanistic account.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering reduces language-induced intuitive answering): Tests the steerability claim. Data: 800 held-out items (item-disjoint from probe training) in the languages showing highest intuitive responding in Experiment 2. Models: same four, frozen; steering adds +beta times the reflection direction in mid layers; beta tuned on a 200-item dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: no-steer, random-direction steering (matched norm), and reflection-direction steering. Decisive metric first: change in Intuition Index; secondary: fluency (external-LM perplexity) and answer-language fidelity. Convincing result: reflection-direction steering lowers the lure rate significantly more than random-direction steering (95% CI on the difference excluding zero) without degrading fluency (perplexity within 5% of no-steer) or answer-language fidelity (>=95%). Indecision band: steering effect within 1 point of the random-direction control - steering does not causally isolate reflection. Negative result (no reduction, or fluency collapse): the direction is not a usable causal lever. Ablations (Experiment 6): layer/strength sweeps and cross-lingual generalization of the direction (train the probe on English, test cross-lingually); convincing if the English-trained direction still reduces lure rate in other languages, indecisive if it transfers only within language family, negative if it fails to transfer. All numbers are planned evidence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Translation artifacts could create item difficulty differences that masquerade as strategy shifts; mitigated by back-translation checks, human verification on a sample, and controlling for per-language accuracy in the dissociation analysis. (2) Intuitive-lure rate among errors can be noisy if accuracy is very high or very low in some languages; we design items calibrated to mid-range difficulty and report confidence intervals. (3) The 'reflection direction' may entangle with content or difficulty rather than a genuine strategy axis; mitigated with matched-item contrasts (same problem, differing only in lure salience) and random-direction controls. (4) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes. (5) The System-1/System-2 framing is a useful abstraction, not a literal claim about LLM cognition; we frame findings behaviorally and mechanistically rather than as evidence of human-like dual processing. (6) A null result (language does not shift the intuition axis beyond accuracy) is still informative, showing multilingual differences are purely competence-driven.

Name: token_granularity_reasoning_tradeoff
Title: The Granularity Tax: When Coarse Tokenization Buys Fluency at the Cost of Compositional Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: The token granularity at which a concept is encoded controls a fundamental trade-off in LLMs: coarse (multi-character, whole-word) tokens improve fluency and retrieval but suppress the compositional/algorithmic reasoning that requires manipulating a concept's internal parts. Crucially, this trade-off is not a fixed property of the tokenizer but is dynamically re-negotiated inside the model, and we can measure a per-concept 'granularity depth' at which sub-token structure becomes accessible and causally intervene on it to trade fluency for reasoning at inference time, without retraining.
Related Work: A cluster of recent work establishes that tokenization harms character-level and arithmetic reasoning: character understanding emerges late and depends on vocabulary size (The Strawberry Problem, 2025; How Do LMs Acquire Character-Level Information, 2026), spelling knowledge is reconstructed in intermediate layers with a 'breakthrough layer' (Spelling-out is not Straightforward, 2025), and tokenization bounds symbolic/arithmetic reasoning even with CoT (Tokenization Constraints, 2025; Tokenization counts, 2024; Counting Ability and Tokenization, 2024). Separately, scaling-law work argues LARGER vocabularies (coarser tokens) improve overall performance (Scaling Laws with Vocabulary, 2024; Over-Tokenized Transformer, 2025). These two literatures are in tension but never reconciled: the first says coarse tokens hurt reasoning, the second says coarse tokens help. No prior work (a) frames these as a single controllable trade-off along a granularity axis, (b) measures WHERE in depth sub-token structure is re-exposed as a per-concept quantity ('granularity depth'), or (c) offers a training-free inference-time intervention that shifts a model along the fluency-vs-reasoning trade-off by amplifying sub-token reconstruction. We reconcile the tension and turn it into a controllable lever.
Abstract: Two recent threads of tokenization research point in opposite directions: one shows that coarse subword tokens cripple character-level and symbolic reasoning, while scaling-law work shows that larger vocabularies (coarser tokens) improve overall model performance. We argue these are two faces of a single phenomenon we call the granularity tax: encoding a concept in a coarse token improves fluent retrieval but hides the concept's internal parts, suppressing the compositional reasoning that must manipulate those parts. We make three contributions. First, we show empirically that for the SAME underlying string, forcing coarse vs. fine tokenization produces a systematic fluency-up / compositional-reasoning-down trade-off across arithmetic, spelling, anagram, and morphological tasks. Second, we introduce granularity depth: using probing classifiers we measure, per concept, the layer at which a coarse token's sub-token structure becomes linearly decodable, and show it is later for higher-frequency/coarser tokens, quantifying an internal 're-negotiation' of granularity. Third, we introduce a training-free intervention, Sub-Token Reconstruction Steering (STRS): we identify the direction along which sub-token structure is written into the residual stream at the breakthrough layer and amplify it during inference. We show STRS shifts a model along the trade-off curve, recovering compositional-reasoning accuracy on coarse-token inputs at a measurable, tunable cost to fluency, and compare it against CoT, single-digit tokenization, and re-tokenization baselines across several open-weight models. Our work unifies conflicting tokenization findings into one controllable axis and provides both a diagnostic (granularity depth) and a lever (STRS) linking token granularity to machine reasoning.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - The granularity trade-off: coarse tokens buy fluency, cost compositional reasoning): Tests the core trade-off. Data: a built matched battery where each item's identical underlying content is presented at coarse vs. fine granularity - (a) multi-digit arithmetic (whole-number tokens vs. comma/space-separated single digits), (b) spelling/letter-counting (whole-word token vs. spelled-out), (c) anagram/character-reordering, (d) morphological segmentation (whole word vs. morpheme-spaced); ~1,000 items per task (4,000 total), length-controlled so coarse/fine pairs differ only in granularity, using right-to-left/comma conventions from prior arithmetic work. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Pythia (1.4B/6.9B) for a scale sweep, all weights frozen; greedy plus 5 samples (temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2). Systems compared: coarse vs. fine presentation of the same content. Decisive metric first: compositional-reasoning accuracy (exact match) as a function of token coarseness; secondary: a fluency proxy (perplexity / log-prob of natural continuations plus a judged generation-quality check on 200 held-out prose samples). Convincing result: a within-item crossover - fine tokenization raises compositional accuracy by >=10 points while coarse tokenization raises the fluency proxy, with both CIs excluding zero, yielding a monotone accuracy-vs-coarseness trade-off curve in at least 3 of 4 model families. Indecision band: accuracy difference between coarse and fine in [0,5] points with CI spanning zero - granularity does not measurably trade off against reasoning, so the 'granularity tax' is not observable behaviorally. Negative result (coarse tokens equal or beat fine on compositional accuracy): no tax; the hypothesis is refuted.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Granularity depth is measurable and later for coarser tokens): Tests that sub-token structure is re-exposed at a per-concept depth. Data: a built probe set of ~2,000 tokens spanning frequency deciles and lengths (from the model vocabulary and a reference corpus for frequency), each presented in a spelling/decomposition prompt. Models: same families, frozen; trainable component is per-layer linear probes decoding the i-th character/sub-token constituent (seeds 0/1/2, 5-fold CV). Systems compared: decoding accuracy across layers; granularity depth = earliest layer whose decoding accuracy exceeds a fixed threshold (e.g., 80%). Decisive metric first: correlation between granularity depth and token frequency/length/vocabulary rank (mixed-effects: depth ~ frequency + length + rank + (1|model)). Convincing result: coarser/higher-frequency tokens have significantly later granularity depth (frequency coefficient CI excluding zero), and the measured breakthrough layer matches prior spelling-reconstruction findings within a few layers. Indecision band: frequency/length coefficients with CIs spanning zero - granularity depth exists but is not systematically organized by coarseness, weakening the 're-negotiation' account. Negative result (sub-token structure decodable everywhere or nowhere): no meaningful granularity-depth variable.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Granularity depth predicts compositional failure): Links the diagnostic to behavior. Data: the 4,000 items from Experiment 1, tagged with the granularity depth of their relevant token from Experiment 2. Models: same, frozen. Decisive metric first: the granularity-depth coefficient in a mixed-effects logistic regression (accuracy ~ granularity_depth + token_length + frequency + (1|model)). Convincing result: later granularity depth predicts lower compositional accuracy (coefficient CI excluding zero) beyond length and frequency. Indecision band: coefficient CI spanning zero - depth is not the operative bottleneck. Negative result (positive coefficient): depth is unrelated to or protective against failure, decoupling the diagnostic from the tax.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Sub-Token Reconstruction Steering shifts the model along the trade-off): Tests the training-free lever. Data: 800 held-out coarse-token items from the Experiment-1 tasks. Models: same, frozen; at the breakthrough layer we compute a difference-in-means reconstruction direction between activations where sub-token structure is decodable vs. not (matched contrast pairs) and amplify it at inference; strength swept, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: (i) no intervention, (ii) CoT prompting, (iii) forced fine tokenization (single-digit/spelled-out), (iv) random-direction steering (matched norm), (v) re-tokenization, and STRS. Decisive metric first: area under the accuracy-vs-fluency trade-off curve - compositional accuracy recovered per unit fluency lost, swept over steering strength; secondary: absolute accuracy gain on coarse inputs and answer fidelity. Convincing result: STRS recovers coarse-input compositional accuracy along a tunable curve, beating random-direction steering (accuracy-per-fluency CI excluding zero) and approaching forced fine tokenization without re-tokenizing. Indecision band: STRS indistinguishable from random-direction steering (difference CI spanning zero) - sub-token structure cannot be cheaply amplified, so the tax is intrinsic rather than a readout artifact (the diagnostic and trade-off findings still stand). Negative result (STRS only degrades the model at all strengths): no usable lever.

Experiment 5 (Scale/emergence sweep): Data: Experiments 1-2 sets. Models: Pythia intermediate training checkpoints and the 1.4B/6.9B sizes, frozen. Decisive metric: the training step / scale at which the granularity tax (Experiment 1 crossover) and STRS recoverability (Experiment 4) first appear. Convincing result: both emerge together at an identifiable scale/step, tying the tax to representational maturity. Indecision band: noisy, non-monotone emergence - we report trajectories descriptively without a claim about onset. Negative result: no consistent emergence pattern. All quantities above are planned evidence, not measured; CIs are bootstrap over items and seeds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Coarse vs. fine presentations may differ in more than granularity (e.g., sequence length, digit ordering); we length-control and use right-to-left/comma conventions from prior arithmetic work to isolate granularity. (2) The 'fluency' proxy (perplexity) may not fully capture generation quality; we supplement with a judged generation-quality check. (3) The reconstruction direction may be entangled with content; we use matched contrast pairs and random-direction controls. (4) STRS may broadly degrade the model if amplified too strongly; the point is a tunable trade-off, so we report the full strength sweep rather than a single operating point. (5) Granularity depth probing can be noisy for rare tokens; we report CIs and restrict to well-attested tokens. (6) A null STRS result (structure cannot be cheaply amplified) is still informative, confirming the tax is intrinsic rather than a readout artifact, and the trade-off characterization and granularity-depth diagnostic stand independently.

Name: verbal_interference_llm
Title: Verbal Interference in LLMs: Using a Concurrent Linguistic Load to Reveal Which Reasoning Depends on Language
Short Hypothesis: Just as concurrent verbal load selectively impairs language-dependent (but not language-independent) reasoning in humans, forcing an LLM to simultaneously generate fluent surface language while it reasons will selectively degrade tasks that recruit shared language-production machinery, and this selective impairment reveals a measurable, task-graded dissociation between an LLM's 'language system' and its reasoning.
Related Work: Two literatures bear on this. (1) LLM latent/implicit reasoning: Coconut (Reasoning Beyond Words, 2024), implicit CoT distillation (2023/2024), latent-CoT mechanistic studies (2025/2026), and SAE-based latent reasoning features (2026) all study REMOVING or REPLACING verbalization to see if reasoning survives in continuous space. (2) Cognitive neuroscience: verbal-interference/dual-task paradigms (Verbal interference paradigms, 2022) show that occupying the language system with a concurrent verbal task selectively impairs cognition that recruits language, and fMRI dissociation studies (The boundaries of language and thought, 2009; Intuitive physical reasoning, 2024; A human brain network for abstract formal reasoning, 2025) show formal/physical reasoning dissociates from the language network. No prior LLM work imports the LOADING logic of verbal interference: instead of ablating language components, we occupy the language-production pathway with a concurrent fluent-generation demand and measure which reasoning tasks are selectively taxed. This directly and behaviorally tests the language-vs-thought dissociation in LLMs and mechanistically localizes the shared bottleneck, distinguishing it from ablation-based and latent-reasoning studies which manipulate the substrate rather than compete for it.
Abstract: In humans, a classic way to test whether a cognitive task depends on language is verbal interference: participants perform a task while a concurrent verbal load occupies the language system, and tasks that recruit language are selectively impaired. Neuroscience shows that formal, logical, and physical reasoning dissociate from the language network, while other cognition (e.g., verbal memory, categorization) does not. We import this loading paradigm into large language models to ask which forms of machine reasoning depend on the language-production pathway. We introduce Concurrent Linguistic Load (CLL): the model is required to interleave, token-by-token or step-by-step, its reasoning with the generation of fluent, semantically demanding but task-irrelevant surface text (e.g., continuing a florid narrative), imposing sustained demand on language production. We measure how much CLL degrades accuracy across a battery of reasoning tasks spanning a hypothesized language-dependence gradient: verbal/word-problem reasoning, arithmetic, symbolic logic, spatial/relational reasoning, and pattern-matrix tasks. Our central prediction is a task-by-load interaction: language-heavy tasks are selectively impaired by CLL relative to control loads (a non-linguistic counting load, or a length-matched inert load), whereas abstract symbolic/spatial tasks are relatively spared. We then localize the shared bottleneck by measuring, under CLL, competition in language-production components (attention heads and MLP neurons identified via next-token fluency contributions) and test whether the size of a task's CLL cost predicts its overlap with language-production circuitry. Across several open-weight models we quantify the interference gradient, control-load specificity, and circuit-overlap correlation. This reframes 'does an LLM think in language?' as an empirically testable, task-graded dissociation.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Task battery with a language-dependence gradient): Prerequisite. Data: ~200 items each for (a) verbal GSM-style word problems (adapted from GSM8K's 1,319-item test set), (b) numeric-only arithmetic (built), (c) propositional/symbolic logic (built), (d) spatial/relational reasoning (adapted from BIG-Bench spatial and relational-ordering tasks), (e) abstract pattern/matrix tasks (adapted from ARC-style and symbolic sequence-completion sets); 1,000 items total, calibrated to mid-range baseline accuracy so interference has room to show. Decisive metric first: per-task no-load baseline accuracy in the 40-85% window. Convincing result: all five tasks fall in that window on the target models, enabling sensitive interaction tests. Indecision band: a task at 85-95% baseline - near ceiling, reducing power; we add harder items. Negative result (a task at ceiling/floor): it is rebalanced or dropped.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Concurrent Linguistic Load selectively degrades language-dependent reasoning): The central dissociation test. Data: the 1,000 items above, used across four load conditions: (i) no-load baseline; (ii) Concurrent Linguistic Load (CLL) - the model interleaves each reasoning step with a fixed quota of fluent, task-irrelevant narrative continuation; (iii) non-linguistic control load - interleave a numeric counting/tally task matched for token quota; (iv) inert control load - interleave copying a fixed filler string (matched length). Loads are imposed by structured prompting that alternates reasoning and load spans with strict format/quota enforcement. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B (scale), all weights frozen; 5 samples/item, temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: the four load conditions across the five task types. Decisive metric first: the task_type x load_condition interaction coefficient from a mixed-effects logistic regression (accuracy ~ task_type * load_condition + (1|model) + (1|item)). Convincing result: CLL's accuracy drop is significantly larger for verbal/word-problem and verbal-logic tasks than for numeric arithmetic and abstract spatial/matrix tasks, and larger than the drop under the non-linguistic and inert control loads (95% CI on the relevant interaction contrasts excluding zero) in at least 3 of 4 models; a compliance check confirms the load task was actually performed (load-span fluency/accuracy above a floor) so drops are not task abandonment. Indecision band: the CLL-specific interaction contrast CI spanning zero (CLL degrades all tasks about equally, like the inert load) - interference is non-specific, so no language-vs-thought dissociation is revealed. Negative result (abstract tasks degrade more than verbal tasks under CLL): the predicted gradient is reversed, refuting the shared-language-bottleneck account.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Interference scales with genuine linguistic demand): Rules out mere token overhead. Data: the verbal and word-problem items under graded CLL - short vs. long, and coherent narrative vs. word-salad - matched for token count; ~400 items x 4 CLL variants. Models: same, frozen. Decisive metric first: slope of CLL cost vs. genuine language-production demand (coherent-narrative load minus matched word-salad/overhead load). Convincing result: interference grows with coherent linguistic demand beyond token-count-matched non-linguistic overhead (slope CI excluding zero). Indecision band: slope CI spanning zero - cost tracks token overhead, not linguistic demand, so 'linguistic' interference is not established. Negative result: word-salad interferes as much as coherent narrative, indicating a generic-capacity, not language-specific, bottleneck.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Behavioral CLL cost tracks language-production circuit overlap): Tests the mechanistic prediction. Data: the 1,000 items; language-production components S_lang per model identified by their contribution to next-token fluency on fluent-continuation spans (attribution/logit-lens), and each reasoning task's causally-important components localized by activation patching on no-load correct-vs-incorrect contrasts (400 items/task). Models: same, frozen; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: per-task behavioral CLL cost vs. per-task Jaccard overlap with S_lang. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation across tasks between CLL cost and S_lang overlap; secondary: measured competition in S_lang (change in activation norm/attention allocation during reasoning spans under CLL vs. no-load). Convincing result: positive CLL-cost-to-overlap correlation (95% CI excluding zero) and measurable S_lang competition under CLL, so the tasks hurt most are those reusing language-production circuitry. Indecision band: correlation CI spanning zero with |rho|<0.3 - behavioral interference is not explained by circuit overlap, leaving the mechanism unlocated even if the behavioral dissociation holds. Negative result (negative correlation): the tasks that share language circuitry are the least hurt, contradicting the loading account. All effect sizes carry bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models; every number is planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) CLL may degrade all tasks non-specifically via added context length/format burden; mitigated by length-matched non-linguistic and inert control loads and by testing the task x load INTERACTION rather than raw drops. (2) The model may abandon the load to protect the reasoning task (or vice versa), confounding interpretation; we monitor load-task compliance and analyze only compliant trials. (3) Even 'non-linguistic' loads pass through the same tokenizer/decoder, so control loads are not perfectly language-free; we use the graded load-quality manipulation to isolate the effect of genuine linguistic demand. (4) Task-type language-dependence labels are hypotheses; a flat interference gradient would itself be an informative result (reasoning shares one bottleneck regardless of surface form). (5) Language-production component identification is noisy; we report multiple models and use overlap correlations rather than single-component claims. (6) Prompt-based interleaving is imperfect control over 'concurrency' compared to true dual-tasking; we treat CLL as an operationalization and note this framing limitation explicitly.

Name: categorical_warping_llm
Title: Categorical Warping: Can an Ad-Hoc Label Scheme Causally Reshape What an LLM Can Discriminate?
Short Hypothesis: A core Whorfian claim is that the categories a language provides warp perception of within-category vs. across-category differences (compression within, expansion across a boundary). We hypothesize that this warping is a dynamic, controllable property of a trained LLM: introducing a novel, ad-hoc labeling scheme in-context causally compresses the model's internal representation of items sharing a new label and expands the gap across new label boundaries, and that this induced geometric warp measurably changes the model's fine-grained discrimination and relational reasoning on the very same items — even when the labels are meaningless nonce words with no pretraining semantics.
Related Work: Cognitive science establishes categorical perception and label-feedback effects, framing them as inference under uncertainty (Cibelli/Regier, 2016/2017; Lupyan, 2012). A deep-learning account (2021) shows fine- vs coarse-grained labels distort semantic geometry, but by *training* a network on those labels. In LLMs, BICAUSE (2025) shows language internalizes causal-order biases and Sapir-Whorf-reproduction studies (2025) probe behavioral alignment; 'When Less Language is More' (2025) ablates language components to help reasoning; number-geometry work (2025/2026) characterizes fixed relational structure. All existing LLM work is observational on *pretrained* vocabularies (color, number, causal order) or removes language rather than adding new categories. No prior work asks whether an *arbitrary, in-context ad-hoc labeling scheme* can causally rewarp an already-trained model's discrimination geometry within a single forward pass, dissociates this from pretrained label semantics using nonce labels, or links the induced geometric warp to changes in downstream relational reasoning. We turn linguistic relativity into a controllable, mechanistic intervention.
Abstract: Linguistic relativity predicts that the category boundaries a language supplies warp cognition: items sharing a label are perceived as more similar (within-category compression) and items across a boundary as more different (across-category expansion). Prior LLM studies test this observationally on pretrained vocabularies (color, causal order). We ask a sharper, causal question: can an arbitrary labeling scheme, introduced only in-context, dynamically rewarp what an already-trained LLM can discriminate and reason about? We construct continuous, controllable stimulus spaces (e.g., numeric magnitudes, HSL colors described in text, feature-vector 'creatures') and impose novel partitions via labels, including nonce labels with no pretraining meaning. Measuring representational distances in hidden states, we test whether presenting a labeling scheme compresses same-label pairs and expands different-label pairs relative to a no-label baseline, and whether the boundary location tracks the arbitrary partition we chose rather than any pretrained structure. We then test behavioral consequences: does the induced warp make the model worse at fine within-category discrimination and better/worse at across-boundary comparisons on identical items? Finally, we test the mechanism causally: we isolate a 'label-warp direction' and steer along it to reproduce or cancel the geometric warp and its behavioral signature, and compare it to an inference-time analog of coarse vs. fine labeling pressure. Across several open-weight models we quantify the compression/expansion index, boundary-placement fidelity to arbitrary partitions, the label-warp-to-behavior correlation, and steering controllability. This reframes linguistic relativity in LLMs from a fixed bias into a controllable, mechanistically-grounded lever on machine discrimination.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Continuous stimulus spaces and label schemes): Prerequisite. Data: three built spaces with ground-truth metric structure - (a) integer magnitudes 1-100, (b) colors specified as HSL text (hue 0-360), (c) synthetic 'creatures' defined by 4 continuous features; for each we prepare no-label, real-word-label, and nonce-word-label (e.g., 'blicket','dax') conditions plus multiple arbitrary boundary placements so a given item pair is same-label under one scheme and different-label under another, and a scrambled-label control (labels assigned randomly to items). ~600 item pairs per space, length/format-matched across conditions. Decisive metric first: verification that schemes are format-matched and that swapped partitions truly cross-classify the same pairs. Convincing result: every target pair appears as both same-label and different-label across schemes; else pairs are regenerated. Indecision/negative bands are design checks, not hypotheses.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Ad-hoc labels causally rewarp discrimination geometry, boundary follows the imposed partition, even for nonce labels): The central Whorfian-warp test. Data: the pairs above, used as is. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and a larger model (Qwen2.5-14B) for scale, all weights frozen. We prompt with the labeling scheme in-context, present item pairs, and extract each item's hidden state at matched positions per layer. Systems compared: no-label baseline, real-word labels, nonce labels, swapped arbitrary partitions, coarse vs. fine schemes, and scrambled-label control. Decisive metric first: the same_label coefficient in a regression of representational distance on true metric gap and a same-label indicator (distance ~ metric_gap + same_label + (1|layer) + (1|model)) - the Compression-Expansion Index. Convincing result: a significant negative same_label coefficient (within-label compression) with boundary-aligned across-label expansion, present even for nonce labels, that REVERSES when the same items are re-partitioned by a different arbitrary scheme (sign flip CI excluding zero), while the scrambled-label control shows no warp; coarse schemes converge items and fine schemes differentiate them, matching the labeling-geometry prediction. Indecision band: same_label coefficient CI spanning zero, or a warp that does not follow the swapped partition - in-context labels do not reliably rewarp geometry, so category structure looks rigidly pretrained rather than dynamically Whorfian. Negative result (positive same_label coefficient, or nonce labels show no effect while only real words do): no genuine categorical warp beyond lexical priming, refuting the causal claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - The warp changes behavior and behavior tracks geometry): Tests downstream consequences. Data: the same items rendered as (i) fine within-category discrimination (which of two same-label items is larger/redder?), (ii) across-boundary comparison, (iii) odd-one-out and analogy tasks; item spacing calibrated to mid-range difficulty to avoid ceiling/floor. Models: same four, frozen; 5 samples/item, temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: imposed scheme vs. no-label baseline. Decisive metric first: change in within-category discrimination accuracy under an imposed scheme; secondary: the mixed-effects correlation between per-pair behavioral change and per-pair measured geometric warp. Convincing result: within-category discrimination degrades and across-boundary judgments shift under an imposed scheme (accuracy-change CI excluding zero), and per-pair behavioral change correlates with geometric warp (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: behavioral-change CI spanning zero while geometry warps - the geometric warp has no behavioral teeth, so the phenomenon is representational-only. Negative result (no behavioral change or negative geometry-behavior correlation): warp does not shape discrimination.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A label-warp direction steers the warp and its behavior on and off): Tests causal controllability. Data: contrast pairs (same items, labeled vs. unlabeled) to compute a mid-layer difference-in-means 'label-warp direction'; 400 held-out pairs per space for evaluation. Models: same four, frozen; steering strength tuned on a dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: +direction steering (induce warp without presenting labels), -direction steering (cancel a presented scheme's warp), random-direction steering (matched norm), and no-steer. Decisive metric first: fraction of the Compression-Expansion Index reproduced (by +steering) or cancelled (by -steering) relative to the label-presentation effect; secondary: matched fraction of the behavioral discrimination change. Convincing result: +steering reproduces and -steering cancels a substantial share of both the geometric and behavioral warp, significantly beyond random-direction steering (difference CI excluding zero). Indecision band: recovered/cancelled fraction under 20% and within the random-direction control's CI - the warp is not captured by a single steerable direction. Negative result (steering has no effect or destroys general output): no isolable causal mechanism. All quantities are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over pairs, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) In-context labels may bias representations trivially via lexical priming rather than genuine categorical warping; mitigated by nonce labels, swapped arbitrary partitions of identical items, and scrambled-label controls that isolate the categorical (boundary-structured) component. (2) Hidden-state distances may reflect the prompt's surface tokens rather than the concept; we extract item representations at matched positions and control for true metric gap. (3) Warp effects may be small or layer-specific; we report multiple layers, models, and effect sizes with bootstrap CIs. (4) Behavioral discrimination tasks could be at ceiling/floor for some spaces; we calibrate item spacing to mid-range difficulty. (5) The label-warp direction may entangle with generic content shifts; random-direction and cancellation controls address this. (6) A null result (arbitrary in-context labels do not warp geometry) is itself informative, indicating LLM category structure is rigidly pretrained rather than dynamically Whorfian.

Name: private_speech_zpd
Title: Chain-of-Thought as Private Speech: Testing the Vygotskian Zone of Proximal Development in LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's chain-of-thought behaves like children's private (self-directed) speech: its amount follows an inverted-U over task difficulty (peaking at moderate difficulty), it shifts from overt to abbreviated/covert form as competence rises, and — the key falsifiable claim — it is beneficial only inside a 'zone of proximal development' (moderate difficulty), while being wasteful overhead on easy items and actively interfering on already-mastered ones, so reasoning should be self-regulated by difficulty rather than applied uniformly.
Related Work: Developmental psychology (Vygotsky; Fernyhough) establishes that private speech follows a developmental trajectory: it appears most at intermediate task difficulty, peaks and then internalizes/abbreviates as skill grows, forming a zone of proximal development. Recent cross-domain work shows GPT-4o produces child-like private speech (Private speech: similarities between an LLM and children, 2026) and reviews inner speech as a cognitive tool (Alderson-Day & Fernyhough, 2023). In ML, 'Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning' (2025) reports reasoning-token length rises then falls over fine-tuning (an inverted-U over TRAINING), latent-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024) internalizes CoT, and 'Why think step by step?' (2023) explains WHEN reasoning helps via data locality. However, no prior work (a) tests the inverted-U of reasoning emission as a function of per-item DIFFICULTY (a within-model, inference-time developmental law, not a training-time one), (b) tests the Vygotskian ZPD prediction that forced reasoning hurts at difficulty extremes, or (c) links overt-to-covert abbreviation of CoT to per-item competence. We turn the developmental theory of private speech into concrete, falsifiable predictions about self-regulated inference-time reasoning.
Abstract: Children talk to themselves while solving hard problems, and developmental psychology gives a precise account of this 'private speech': its quantity follows an inverted-U over task difficulty, it is concentrated in a learner's zone of proximal development (ZPD), and it becomes abbreviated and covert as competence grows. We propose that an LLM's chain-of-thought (CoT) is a computational analog of private speech and obeys the same developmental laws — at inference time and per item, not merely over training. We make three falsifiable predictions. (1) Emission: when allowed to reason freely, a model's spontaneous CoT length forms an inverted-U over graded difficulty, peaking at intermediate difficulty rather than rising monotonically. (2) ZPD benefit: the accuracy gain from CoT over direct answering is largest at intermediate difficulty and small or negative at the extremes — forced reasoning is wasteful overhead on trivial items and can interfere on already-mastered items. (3) Abbreviation: as items move from moderate toward mastered, spontaneous CoT compresses (shorter, more elliptical), mirroring overt-to-covert internalization. We test these across difficulty-graded arithmetic, logic, and word-problem suites on several open-weight models with controlled per-item difficulty calibration. We then add a lightweight mechanistic component: a probe that reads a model's own competence/difficulty estimate from early hidden states, used to build a self-regulated 'ZPD-gated' reasoning controller that spends CoT only where it helps, and compare it to always-CoT and never-CoT baselines on accuracy and token cost. Confirming these predictions reframes CoT as difficulty-self-regulated private speech and yields a principled, training-free efficiency lever.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Difficulty-graded task suites with calibrated per-item difficulty): Prerequisite. Data: built suites of ~300 items each - multi-digit arithmetic (operand size/carry count as the surface difficulty axis), propositional/multi-hop logic (number of inference steps), and GSM-style word problems (number of reasoning steps); 900 items. Per-item empirical difficulty = direct-answer error rate estimated from 20 samples/item per model, giving a continuous difficulty score independent of the surface axis. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, all weights frozen, seeds 0/1/2. Decisive metric first: spread and reliability (split-half) of the calibrated difficulty score. Convincing result: difficulty spans a wide range with split-half reliability >=0.7, and is not confounded with item length (|correlation| < 0.3). Indecision band: reliability 0.5-0.7 - we increase samples/item. Negative result (difficulty not separable from length): the calibration is unusable and we redesign items.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Spontaneous reasoning emission forms an inverted-U over difficulty): Tests the emission law. Data: the 900 items, elicited under a permissive prompt that neither forbids nor mandates chain-of-thought. Models: same four, frozen. Systems compared: a quadratic vs. a monotonic model of CoT length over difficulty. Decisive metric first: the sign and significance of the quadratic coefficient in length ~ difficulty + difficulty^2 + (1|model) + (1|item), plus AIC/BIC preference of the quadratic over the monotonic model. Convincing result: a significant negative quadratic term (95% CI excluding zero) with an interior peak at intermediate difficulty, and AIC/BIC favoring the quadratic, in at least 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: quadratic-term CI spanning zero but AIC/BIC roughly tied - emission is not clearly inverted-U (could be monotone or flat), so the private-speech emission law is unsupported at this resolution. Negative result (positive quadratic or strictly monotone increasing length): reasoning emission does not follow the developmental inverted-U.

Experiment 3 (H2 - CoT benefit is a zone-of-proximal-development function of difficulty): Tests the ZPD-benefit claim. Data: the 900 items, each evaluated under forced-direct (no CoT), forced-CoT, and free conditions; 10 samples/condition/item. Models: same four, frozen. Decisive metric first: the per-item CoT benefit = accuracy(CoT) - accuracy(direct), fitted as benefit ~ difficulty + difficulty^2. Convincing result: benefit peaks at intermediate difficulty, is within +/-2 points of zero on easy items, and is significantly negative (interference) on a subset of already-mastered-but-nontrivial items (negative-benefit CI excluding zero), with qualitative confirmation that forced CoT introduces errors the direct answer avoided. Indecision band: benefit rises monotonically with difficulty with no interior peak and no negative region (quadratic CI spanning zero) - CoT is simply more useful on harder items, the ordinary view, and the distinctive ZPD prediction (harm at extremes) fails. Negative result (benefit flat or U-shaped): no ZPD structure.

Experiment 4 (H3 - CoT abbreviates as items approach mastery): Tests the internalization prediction. Data: within a fixed surface-difficulty band, items split into 'newly-in-ZPD' vs. 'approaching-mastery' by per-item direct accuracy; ~300 items/band. Models: same four, frozen. Decisive metric first: spontaneous CoT length; secondary: number of explicit steps and an ellipsis/compression score (operator-to-filler token ratio). Convincing result: CoT shortens and becomes more elliptical as items approach mastery (length and compression CIs excluding zero) within the matched surface band. Indecision band: length difference CI spanning zero with |effect| below one step - no measurable abbreviation. Negative result (CoT lengthens toward mastery): contradicts overt-to-covert internalization.

Experiment 5 (H4 - A self-difficulty probe supports a ZPD-gated controller that beats uniform reasoning): Tests the self-regulation payoff. Data: question-only early-layer hidden states (before any reasoning) for the 900 items, 70/30 item-disjoint split; controller evaluated on 300 held-out items. Models: same four, frozen; trainable component is a lightweight linear probe predicting calibrated difficulty (seeds 0/1/2). Systems compared: always-CoT, never-CoT, random-gated (matched CoT budget), and ZPD-gated (emit CoT only when predicted difficulty is in the middle band). Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token budget (and, jointly, the accuracy-vs-average-tokens frontier); secondary: probe AUROC/correlation for predicting difficulty. Convincing result: ZPD-gating matches or exceeds always-CoT accuracy (its 95% CI lower bound at or above always-CoT) at a fraction of the tokens, and beats random-gating at equal budget (difference CI excluding zero), with probe AUROC >=0.65. Indecision band: ZPD-gating within 1 accuracy point of random-gating at equal budget - the model's internal difficulty estimate adds no usable signal, so the controller is not justified even if the probe is weakly above chance. Negative result (ZPD-gating below never-CoT or below random-gating): self-regulated private speech is not a useful lever. All numbers are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may be strongly primed to always emit CoT, flattening the spontaneous inverted-U; we mitigate with permissive prompts, base/less-aligned models, and by measuring emission via willingness-to-abbreviate rather than raw presence. (2) 'Difficulty' calibrated from direct-answer error may conflate item difficulty with model-specific gaps; we calibrate per-model and also report the surface difficulty axis. (3) The inverted-U could be an artifact of length ceilings (max tokens) or format; we cap generously and length-control. (4) Interference (negative CoT benefit on mastered items) may be small or model-dependent; a monotonic (non-ZPD) result is itself informative, distinguishing LLM reasoning from human private speech. (5) The competence probe may capture surface features rather than genuine self-difficulty estimation; we test generalization across task families and use question-only (pre-reasoning) activations. (6) The developmental/private-speech framing is an analogy operationalized behaviorally, not a claim of human-like inner experience; we frame all findings behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: lexical_gap_resolution
Title: Mind the Gap: Do Lexicalization Gaps in the Latent Pivot Language Blur an LLM's Concepts?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs route non-English inputs through a largely English-shaped 'concept space.' We hypothesize that a concept's internal representational resolution is bottlenecked by whether it is *lexicalized* (has a compact, single-/few-token word) in the model's latent pivot language: concepts that fall in a lexical gap of the pivot language are represented more diffusely, are harder to separate from neighbors, and yield systematically worse fine-grained reasoning — and providing an ad-hoc lexicalization (a coined single token/name) in-context sharpens both the geometry and the behavior.
Related Work: A cluster of work establishes that multilingual LLMs form a shared, largely English-pivoted concept space in middle layers (Semantic Hub Hypothesis 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Tracing Multilingual Representations with Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; When Meanings Meet 2026). These works show a shared space *exists* and can be causally patched, and that averaging concept representations across languages helps translation. Concept Space Alignment (2024) and High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations (2025) show alignment quality varies by typology and abstractness. XCOMPS (2025) shows conceptual understanding degrades for low-resource and morphologically complex languages. Crucially, all this work treats concepts holistically or averages across languages; none isolates *lexicalization gaps* — concepts that are compactly lexicalized in some languages but not the pivot — as a natural, controllable experiment on whether the pivot language's vocabulary sets a resolution limit on non-linguistic conceptual discrimination and reasoning. We uniquely (1) predict a lexicalization-gap penalty on representational resolution and downstream fine-grained reasoning, (2) contrast this with mere frequency/abstractness confounds, and (3) test a causal, training-free 'ad-hoc lexicalization' intervention that closes the gap.
Abstract: Multilingual language models process the world through a shared internal concept space that is disproportionately shaped by their dominant (often English) latent pivot language. We ask a simple question with deep implications for how language bounds machine intelligence: does the *vocabulary* of the pivot language set a resolution limit on what the model can finely discriminate and reason about? Human languages differ in which concepts they lexicalize — some have a single compact word for a notion (e.g., a specific kinship relation, an emotion, a color category, a shade of taste) that other languages must express periphrastically. We hypothesize a lexicalization-gap penalty: concepts that lack a compact lexicalization in the pivot language are represented more diffusely (lower cluster tightness, poorer separability from neighbors) and are correspondingly harder for the model to reason about at fine grain, even when the content is expressed identically. We assemble concept sets that are lexicalized in some languages but constitute lexical gaps in English, matched to lexicalized controls on frequency and abstractness, and measure (i) representational resolution via probing and cluster geometry across layers, and (ii) fine-grained behavioral discrimination and relational reasoning. We then test causality two ways: introducing an ad-hoc single-token lexicalization (a coined name) in-context should sharpen geometry and improve reasoning about gap concepts, while artificially 'de-lexicalizing' control concepts (forcing periphrastic reference) should blur them.
